title: Python Basics: A First Program
author: Asha Rao
content: Python is a high-level programming language known for readable code. A first Python program prints a message with the print function. Python uses indentation instead of braces to group statements, so the layout of the code is part of its meaning. Variables do not need type declarations: Python is dynamically typed, which means the type belongs to the value, not to the variable. The standard library includes modules for files, dates, networking and much more, which is why people say Python comes with batteries included. Python is interpreted: the interpreter compiles source code to bytecode and executes it, so you can experiment interactively in the REPL.

title: Functions and Arguments in Python
author: Asha Rao
content: A function in Python is defined with the def keyword, a name, parameters in parentheses and an indented body. Functions return a value with return; without it they return None. Python supports default argument values, keyword arguments, and variable-length arguments with *args and **kwargs. Functions are first-class objects: you can pass a function as an argument, return it from another function, or store it in a list. A lambda creates a small anonymous function in a single expression. Good functions do one thing, have a clear name, and include a docstring explaining what they do.

title: Python Virtual Environments with venv
author: Girish
content: A virtual environment is an isolated folder that contains its own Python interpreter and installed packages. Create one with python -m venv .venv and activate it before installing anything. Each project gets its own environment, so two projects can depend on different versions of the same library without conflict. pip installs packages into the active virtual environment, and pip freeze or a requirements.txt file records the exact dependencies so others can recreate the environment. On Windows the activation script lives in .venv\Scripts, on Linux and macOS in .venv/bin. Never commit the virtual environment folder to Git; commit requirements.txt instead.

title: Python Decorators Explained
author: Ravi Kumar
content: A decorator is a function that takes another function and returns a new function that adds behaviour. The @ syntax above a def is shorthand for wrapping: @timer above def work is the same as work = timer(work). Decorators are used for logging, timing, caching, access control and registering routes in web frameworks. functools.wraps copies the name and docstring of the original function to the wrapper. The built-in functools.lru_cache decorator memoizes results so repeated calls with the same arguments return instantly.

title: Asynchronous Python with asyncio
author: Ravi Kumar
content: asyncio lets a single Python thread handle many input and output operations at the same time. An async def function is a coroutine; await pauses it until the awaited operation finishes, letting the event loop run other coroutines meanwhile. This is ideal for network servers and web scraping, where programs spend most of their time waiting for responses. asyncio is cooperative multitasking: a coroutine that runs a long CPU-bound loop without awaiting blocks every other task. For CPU-heavy work use processes instead. Frameworks such as FastAPI are built on async Python.

title: Python Lists, Dictionaries, Sets and Tuples
author: Asha Rao
content: Python has four core built-in data structures. A list is an ordered, mutable sequence; appending is fast but searching for a value scans the whole list. A tuple is like a list but immutable. A dictionary maps keys to values using a hash table, so looking up a key takes constant time on average. A set stores unique values and supports fast membership tests and set operations such as union and intersection. Choosing the right data structure is often the biggest performance decision in a Python program.

title: Java Fundamentals
author: Meera Iyer
content: Java is a statically typed, object-oriented programming language. Every Java program is organised into classes, and execution starts in a public static void main method. Java source code is compiled by javac into bytecode, which runs on the Java Virtual Machine, so the same compiled program runs on any operating system with a JVM: write once, run anywhere. Java requires explicit types for variables, catches many errors at compile time, and is widely used for enterprise backends and Android applications.

title: Garbage Collection in the JVM
author: Meera Iyer
content: The Java Virtual Machine manages memory automatically through garbage collection. Objects are allocated on the heap, and the garbage collector reclaims objects that are no longer reachable from any live reference. Most JVM collectors are generational: new objects are created in the young generation, where most die quickly, and survivors are promoted to the old generation. Minor collections clean the young generation often and cheaply; major collections of the old generation are rarer and slower. Modern collectors such as G1 and ZGC aim for short pause times so applications stay responsive.

title: The Java Collections Framework
author: Meera Iyer
content: The Java Collections Framework provides interfaces and implementations for groups of objects. List implementations include ArrayList, backed by a resizable array, and LinkedList. Set implementations such as HashSet store unique elements, and TreeSet keeps them sorted. Map implementations associate keys with values: HashMap offers constant-time average lookups, while TreeMap keeps keys sorted using a red-black tree. Generics let collections declare the type of element they hold, so type errors are caught by the compiler.

title: Java vs Python: Which Should You Learn First?
author: Ravi Kumar
content: Java and Python are both popular first languages, but they feel different. Python code is shorter and dynamically typed, which makes it quick for scripting, data science and machine learning. Java is statically typed and more verbose, which helps large teams catch mistakes early and makes it common in enterprise systems and Android development. Python is usually interpreted while Java compiles to bytecode for the JVM, so Java programs often run faster. For beginners Python has a gentler learning curve; for understanding types and object-oriented design, Java is excellent.

title: SQL Basics: SELECT, WHERE and JOIN
author: Kiran Shetty
content: SQL is the standard language for relational databases. SELECT chooses columns, FROM names the table, and WHERE filters rows. ORDER BY sorts the result and LIMIT restricts how many rows are returned. A JOIN combines rows from two tables using a related column, for example orders and customers joined on customer_id. GROUP BY with aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM and AVG summarises data. INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change data. SQL is declarative: you describe the result you want and the database decides how to compute it.

title: How Database Indexes Work: B-Trees
author: Kiran Shetty
content: A database index is a separate data structure that makes lookups fast. Without an index, a query that filters on a column must read every row: a full table scan. Most relational databases store indexes as B-trees, balanced trees whose nodes hold many sorted keys, so finding a key takes only a few disk reads even for millions of rows. An index speeds up WHERE filters, joins and ORDER BY on the indexed column, but it costs disk space and slows down inserts and updates, because every index must be updated too. Composite indexes cover several columns; the column order matters.

title: ACID Transactions Explained
author: Kiran Shetty
content: A transaction groups several database operations into one unit of work. ACID describes the guarantees a transaction provides. Atomicity: all operations succeed or none take effect; a failure rolls everything back. Consistency: the database moves from one valid state to another, respecting constraints. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work. Durability: once committed, changes survive crashes, typically thanks to a write-ahead log. Transferring money between bank accounts is the classic example: debiting one account and crediting the other must happen together or not at all.

title: Database Normalization: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF
content: Normalization organises tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies. First normal form requires atomic values: no lists inside a column. Second normal form removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key. Third normal form removes transitive dependencies, so non-key columns depend only on the key. A normalised schema stores each fact once, which prevents inconsistent copies. Sometimes designers denormalise on purpose to make frequent read queries faster, accepting some duplication.

title: NoSQL Databases: Documents, Key-Value and Graphs
author: Ravi Kumar
content: NoSQL databases drop the relational table model to gain flexibility or scale. Document databases such as MongoDB store JSON-like documents with flexible fields. Key-value stores such as Redis map keys to values and are extremely fast, often used for caching and sessions. Wide-column stores such as Cassandra spread data across many machines. Graph databases store nodes and relationships, which suits social networks and recommendation. Many NoSQL systems trade strict consistency for availability and horizontal scaling.

title: SQLite: A Database in a Single File
author: Girish
content: SQLite is an embedded relational database: the whole database is one ordinary file and the engine runs inside your application, with no separate server process. It supports most of SQL, transactions with full ACID guarantees, indexes, triggers and views. Write-ahead logging mode lets readers continue while a writer commits. SQLite is used in phones, browsers, desktop applications and small websites. Python includes it in the standard library as the sqlite3 module, which makes it an excellent first database for projects.

title: Processes and Threads
author: Meera Iyer
content: A process is a running program with its own address space, open files and resources. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process; threads of the same process share memory, which makes communication fast but requires synchronisation with locks to avoid race conditions. Creating a process is more expensive than creating a thread, and switching between processes costs more because the memory mappings change. The operating system scheduler decides which thread runs on each CPU core. Python has a global interpreter lock, so CPU-bound Python code uses multiple processes for parallelism.

title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms
content: The CPU scheduler picks which ready process runs next. First-come first-served is simple but short jobs can wait behind long ones. Shortest job first minimises average waiting time but needs to know job lengths in advance. Round robin gives each process a fixed time slice, or quantum, and rotates through the ready queue, which keeps interactive systems responsive. Priority scheduling runs important processes first; aging gradually raises the priority of waiting processes to prevent starvation. Real operating systems combine these ideas in multilevel feedback queues.

title: Virtual Memory and Paging
author: Meera Iyer
content: Virtual memory gives each process the illusion of a large, private, contiguous address space. The address space is divided into fixed-size pages, and physical memory into frames of the same size. A page table maps virtual pages to physical frames, and the translation lookaside buffer caches recent translations. When a process touches a page that is not in physical memory, a page fault occurs and the operating system loads the page from disk, possibly evicting another page using a replacement policy such as least recently used. Too many page faults cause thrashing.

title: Deadlocks: Conditions, Prevention and Avoidance
author: Kiran Shetty
content: A deadlock happens when a set of processes each wait for a resource held by another process in the set, so none can continue. Four conditions must all hold: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Prevention breaks one condition, for example by always acquiring locks in a fixed global order, which removes circular wait. Avoidance, such as the banker's algorithm, grants a request only if the system stays in a safe state. Detection lets deadlocks happen, finds cycles in the wait-for graph, and recovers by terminating a process.

title: How File Systems Organise Data
content: A file system organises data on a disk into files and directories. Metadata such as size, permissions and timestamps is stored in structures like inodes, which also point to the disk blocks that hold the file contents. Directories map names to inodes. Journaling file systems such as ext4 and NTFS write intended changes to a journal first, so after a crash the disk can be repaired quickly instead of scanning everything. Fragmentation spreads a file across distant blocks and slows down reading on spinning disks.

title: The OSI Model: Seven Network Layers
author: Kiran Shetty
content: The OSI model splits computer networking into seven layers. Physical carries bits over cables or radio. Data link moves frames between neighbouring devices using MAC addresses. Network routes packets between networks using IP addresses. Transport provides end-to-end delivery, with TCP or UDP. Session, presentation and application handle conversations, data formats and the protocols programs use, such as HTTP and DNS. The simpler TCP/IP model merges these into four layers, but the OSI vocabulary is still used to describe where a problem occurs.

title: TCP vs UDP: Reliable or Fast?
author: Ravi Kumar
content: TCP and UDP are the two main transport protocols. TCP is connection-oriented: a three-way handshake sets up the connection, every segment is acknowledged, lost data is retransmitted, and bytes arrive in order. TCP also controls congestion so it does not overwhelm the network. UDP sends independent datagrams with no handshake, no acknowledgements and no ordering, which makes it lighter and faster. Web pages, email and file transfers use TCP; live video, voice calls, online games and DNS queries often use UDP, where a late packet is worse than a lost one.

title: How DNS Resolution Works
content: The Domain Name System translates names like example.com into IP addresses. When you visit a site, your computer asks a recursive resolver, usually run by your internet provider. If the answer is not cached, the resolver asks a root server, which points to the top-level domain servers for .com, which point to the authoritative name server for example.com, which returns the address. Each answer has a time to live, so resolvers cache it to make later lookups fast. Record types include A for IPv4 addresses, AAAA for IPv6 and MX for mail servers.

title: HTTP: Requests, Responses and Status Codes
author: Asha Rao
content: HTTP is the protocol browsers and servers use to exchange web pages and data. A client sends a request with a method such as GET or POST, a path and headers; the server replies with a status code, headers and a body. Status codes are grouped: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client errors such as 404 Not Found, and 5xx server errors. HTTP is stateless, so cookies or tokens are used to remember users between requests. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, which encrypts the connection and verifies the server's identity.

title: IP Addressing and Routing
content: Every device on an IP network has an address. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written as four numbers such as 192.168.1.10; IPv6 uses 128 bits to solve address exhaustion. A subnet mask divides an address into network and host parts. Routers forward packets hop by hop, choosing the next hop from a routing table built by protocols such as OSPF inside an organisation and BGP between internet providers. Private address ranges are not routed on the public internet; network address translation lets many private devices share one public address.

title: Introduction to Machine Learning
author: Girish
content: Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence in which programs learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules. A model is trained on examples, its parameters are adjusted to reduce a loss function, and it is then used to make predictions on new data. The main families are supervised learning, unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning. Machine learning powers spam filters, recommendations, speech recognition and image classification. Good data matters more than clever algorithms: a model can only learn what its training data shows.

title: Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning
author: Ravi Kumar
content: In supervised learning every training example has a label, and the model learns to map inputs to labels: classification predicts categories such as spam or not spam, regression predicts numbers such as house prices. In unsupervised learning there are no labels; the algorithm finds structure on its own, for example clustering customers into groups with k-means or reducing dimensions with principal component analysis. Semi-supervised learning combines a few labelled examples with many unlabelled ones.

title: Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
content: Linear regression models a numeric target as a weighted sum of input features plus a bias. Training finds the weights that minimise the mean squared error between predictions and true values. Gradient descent does this iteratively: compute the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight and take a small step in the opposite direction, scaled by the learning rate. A learning rate that is too large makes training diverge; too small makes it slow. Feature scaling helps gradient descent converge faster.

title: Neural Networks and Backpropagation
author: Girish
content: A neural network is built from layers of artificial neurons. Each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through a non-linear activation function such as ReLU. Stacking layers lets the network learn complex patterns. Training uses backpropagation: the network makes a prediction, a loss measures the error, and the chain rule computes how much each weight contributed to the error, layer by layer from the output backwards. An optimiser such as stochastic gradient descent or Adam then updates the weights. Deep learning means networks with many layers.

title: Overfitting and How to Prevent It
author: Ravi Kumar
content: A model overfits when it memorises the training data, including its noise, and performs poorly on new data. The sign is low training error but high validation error. Remedies include collecting more data, choosing a simpler model, regularization such as L1 and L2 penalties that discourage large weights, dropout in neural networks, and early stopping when validation error starts to rise. Cross-validation estimates how well a model generalises. Underfitting is the opposite problem: the model is too simple to capture the pattern.

title: Decision Trees and Random Forests
content: A decision tree predicts by asking a sequence of yes or no questions about the features, splitting the data at each node to make the groups as pure as possible, measured by Gini impurity or entropy. Trees are easy to interpret but overfit easily when grown deep. A random forest trains many trees on random samples of the data and random subsets of features, then averages their votes, which reduces variance and usually improves accuracy. Gradient boosting builds trees one after another, each correcting the errors of the previous ones.

title: HTML and CSS Fundamentals
author: Asha Rao
content: HTML describes the structure of a web page with elements such as headings, paragraphs, links, images and forms. Semantic elements like header, nav, main, article and footer tell browsers and search engines what each part of the page means. CSS controls presentation: selectors choose elements and declarations set properties such as color, font and margin. Flexbox and grid lay out elements in rows, columns and two-dimensional grids. Media queries adapt the layout to small screens, which is the basis of responsive design.

title: JavaScript and the DOM
content: JavaScript is the programming language of the web browser. The browser turns HTML into the Document Object Model, a tree of objects that JavaScript can read and change. document.querySelector finds elements, addEventListener reacts to clicks and key presses, and changing textContent or classList updates the page without reloading it. The fetch function requests data from a server asynchronously and returns a promise; async and await make that code read top to bottom. Inserting untrusted text with innerHTML can lead to cross-site scripting, so textContent is safer.

title: Designing REST APIs
author: Ravi Kumar
content: A REST API exposes resources at URLs and uses HTTP methods to act on them: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH updates, and DELETE removes. Responses use status codes meaningfully, for example 201 Created, 404 Not Found and 422 for invalid input, and usually carry JSON bodies. Good APIs are consistent in naming, paginate long lists, validate input, and version their interface. Frameworks such as FastAPI generate interactive OpenAPI documentation from type hints, which makes APIs easy to explore and test.

title: React Components and Hooks
content: React builds user interfaces from components: functions that take props and return JSX describing what to render. When state changes, React re-renders the component and updates only the parts of the DOM that differ. The useState hook stores local state and useEffect runs side effects such as fetching data after rendering. Lists need a stable key for each item so React can track them. Lifting state up to a common parent lets sibling components share data. Vite provides a fast development server for React projects.

title: Big-O Notation and Time Complexity
author: Meera Iyer
content: Big-O notation describes how the running time or memory of an algorithm grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constant factors. O(1) is constant time, like reading an array element by index. O(log n) appears when the problem is halved each step, as in binary search. O(n) is linear, such as scanning a list once. O(n log n) is typical of efficient comparison sorting. O(n squared) arises from nested loops over the input. Analysing complexity tells you whether an algorithm will still be fast when the data is a thousand times bigger.

title: Sorting Algorithms Compared
author: Kiran Shetty
content: Bubble sort, selection sort and insertion sort are simple but take O(n squared) time, although insertion sort is fast on nearly sorted data. Merge sort divides the list in half, sorts each half recursively and merges them, always running in O(n log n) time and keeping equal elements in order, which makes it stable. Quicksort picks a pivot and partitions the list around it; it averages O(n log n) and is very fast in practice, but a bad pivot gives O(n squared). Heap sort uses a binary heap and sorts in place in O(n log n). Python's built-in sort uses Timsort, a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort.

title: Binary Search on a Sorted Array
author: Girish
content: Binary search finds a target value in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search interval. Compare the target with the middle element: if equal, you are done; if the target is smaller, continue in the left half, otherwise in the right half. Each step discards half of the remaining elements, so binary search runs in O(log n) time: about twenty comparisons for a million elements. The array must be sorted first. Off-by-one errors in the boundaries are the classic bug. Python's bisect module implements binary search for sorted lists.

title: Graph Traversal: BFS, DFS and Shortest Paths
content: A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges. Breadth-first search explores neighbours level by level using a queue, so in an unweighted graph it finds the shortest path in number of edges. Depth-first search follows one branch as deep as possible before backtracking, using a stack or recursion; it is used for cycle detection and topological sorting. For weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights, Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths using a priority queue. Web crawlers traverse the link graph of the web, usually breadth first.

title: Dynamic Programming for Beginners
author: Ravi Kumar
content: Dynamic programming solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing each subproblem's answer so it is computed only once. Memoization caches the results of recursive calls top down; tabulation fills a table bottom up. The Fibonacci sequence is the classic example: naive recursion takes exponential time, while dynamic programming takes linear time. Other examples include the knapsack problem, longest common subsequence and edit distance, the number of insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to turn one word into another, which spell checkers use.

title: The Inverted Index: How Search Engines Find Documents
author: Girish
content: A search engine cannot read every document for every query. Instead it builds an inverted index: for every term, a postings list of the documents that contain it, often with the term frequency and the positions where the term occurs. Answering a query means looking up each term's postings list and combining them: intersection for AND, union for OR. Positions make phrase search possible. Before indexing, text goes through tokenization, normalization, stop-word removal and stemming, and the same steps are applied to queries so they match the index.

title: Ranking Search Results: TF-IDF and BM25
author: Ravi Kumar
content: Finding matching documents is only half of search; ranking puts the best ones first. TF-IDF scores a document higher when a query term appears often in it, term frequency, and when the term is rare in the collection, inverse document frequency. BM25 improves on TF-IDF in two ways: term frequency saturates, so the tenth occurrence adds little, and scores are normalised by document length, so long documents do not win just because they contain more words. BM25 has two parameters, k1 for saturation and b for length normalisation, and is the default ranking function in many search engines.

title: The Big Computer Science Glossary
content: This glossary collects short definitions of common computer science terms, in alphabetical order, for quick revision before exams and interviews. Algorithm: a step by step procedure. Array: a contiguous block of memory holding elements. Backpropagation: how a neural network computes gradients; a neural network learns with backpropagation, and backpropagation updates the network. Binary search: searching a sorted array by halving; binary search on a sorted array is fast. Cache: a small fast memory. Compiler: translates source code. Database: an organised collection of data; a database stores data, a database index speeds up a database, and database transactions protect a database. Deadlock: processes waiting on each other forever. DNS: the internet's phone book; DNS resolution maps names to addresses. Garbage collection: automatic memory reclamation, as in the JVM; garbage collection in the JVM frees memory. Graph: nodes and edges; graph search finds a shortest path in a graph. Index: a structure for fast lookup; an index makes search fast. Inverted index: term to documents; a search engine uses an inverted index. Java: a language that runs on the JVM. Machine learning: learning from data; machine learning models learn, supervised machine learning uses labels. Network: connected computers; TCP and UDP carry network data. Overfitting: memorising training data; overfitting hurts models, regularization reduces overfitting. Paging: the virtual memory technique; virtual memory uses paging, paging uses page tables. Python: a popular language; Python is used for machine learning, Python has a virtual environment tool, Python has asyncio for async code. Queue: first in first out. Sorting: ordering data; sorting algorithms such as merge sort and quicksort have complexity O(n log n). TCP: reliable transport. Thread: a unit of execution. UDP: fast datagrams, the difference between TCP and UDP is reliability. Virtual environment: an isolated Python installation. That is the end of the glossary; revise it often.
